title: Python asyncio Fundamentals: Handwritten Notes
summary: How single-threaded cooperative concurrency works in Python: coroutines and async/await, the event loop, asyncio.run, the three kinds of awaitable, and how await hands control back to the loop. It also covers keeping blocking calls off the loop with to_thread and run_in_executor, and why asyncio does not make CPU-bound work faster.

chapters.title: Why asyncio? The Concurrency Model
points: Concurrency means juggling many tasks whose progress overlaps. Parallelism means running tasks at the same instant on several cores. asyncio gives you concurrency only.
asyncio is single-threaded cooperative multitasking. A task keeps running until it chooses to give up control at an await.
Preemptive threads can be switched by the OS at any bytecode boundary. asyncio switches happen only at an await you can see in the code.
It fits I/O-bound workloads: network calls, database queries, sockets, and thousands of idle connections that spend most of their time waiting.
Waiting costs almost nothing. While one coroutine waits on a socket, the loop runs other ready coroutines.
Memory: an OS thread reserves about 1-8 MB of stack, while a coroutine object is about 1-2 KB, so 10k concurrent connections are practical.
Few race conditions: code between two awaits is effectively atomic. You still need asyncio.Lock when shared state is updated across an await.
Comparison row, threads: preemptive, cheap to write blocking-style, GIL-bound for Python code, and needs locks everywhere.
Comparison row, processes: true parallelism for CPU work, but heavy to start, and every argument must be pickled across IPC.
Comparison row, asyncio: explicit switch points, the lightest per task, and the whole call chain has to be async ('function colouring').

chapters.title: Coroutines and async / await
points: `async def f():` defines a coroutine function. Calling `f()` does not run the body. It returns a coroutine object.
A coroutine object is a suspendable computation. It runs only when it is awaited, or when it is wrapped in a Task and scheduled on the loop.
`await expr` is only valid inside `async def` (or at the top level of the `python -m asyncio` REPL). Anywhere else it is a SyntaxError.
`await` suspends the current coroutine until the awaitable finishes, then evaluates to its result, or re-raises its exception.
Under the hood coroutines are built on generators: `coro.send(None)` advances the coroutine to its next suspension point, and StopIteration.value carries the return value.
Example: `async def fetch(): await asyncio.sleep(1); return 'data'`, then `result = await fetch()` inside another coroutine.
Also async: `async with` (__aenter__/__aexit__), `async for` (__aiter__/__anext__), and async generators (`async def` containing `yield`).
Mistake: calling `fetch()` without await produces 'RuntimeWarning: coroutine was never awaited', and the body never runs.
Mistake: `await` on an ordinary function's result raises TypeError: object X can't be used in 'await' expression.
Inspection: `inspect.iscoroutinefunction(f)` checks the function and `inspect.iscoroutine(obj)` checks the object. `asyncio.iscoroutine` does the same for the object.

chapters.title: The Event Loop
points: The event loop is the scheduler. It keeps a queue of ready callbacks, a heap of timers, and a set of watched file descriptors.
One iteration: run every ready callback, compute a timeout from the nearest timer, block in the selector until I/O or the timeout, then queue the callbacks that became ready.
The I/O wait uses the OS multiplexer: epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS and BSD, and IOCP through ProactorEventLoop, the Windows default since Python 3.8.
Tasks are driven by callbacks. The loop calls Task.__step(), which advances the coroutine by one `send()`.
There is one running loop per thread. `asyncio.get_running_loop()` returns it and raises RuntimeError when no loop is running.
Loop scheduling APIs: `loop.call_soon(cb)`, `loop.call_later(delay, cb)`, `loop.call_at(when, cb)`, and `loop.call_soon_threadsafe(cb)` for use from other threads.
The loop is not thread-safe. The only safe entry points from another thread are call_soon_threadsafe and `asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe(coro, loop)`.
Debug mode (`asyncio.run(main(), debug=True)` or PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG=1) logs callbacks that run longer than 100 ms and coroutines that were never awaited.
Mistake: `asyncio.get_event_loop()` is deprecated for getting a loop outside a running loop. Inside coroutines, use get_running_loop().
uvloop is a drop-in libuv-based loop and is often about 2-4x faster for network-heavy servers.

chapters.title: asyncio.run: The Entry Point
points: `asyncio.run(main())` is the standard synchronous-to-async bridge. It is normally called once per program.
Step 1: it creates a new event loop and sets it as the current loop for this thread.
Step 2: it runs `main()` until complete and returns its result, or propagates its exception.
Step 3, cleanup: it cancels leftover tasks, runs `loop.shutdown_asyncgens()`, runs `shutdown_default_executor()` (Python 3.9+), and closes the loop.
Example pattern: `async def main(): ...` followed by `if __name__ == '__main__': asyncio.run(main())`.
Calling asyncio.run while a loop is already running (for example inside Jupyter or another coroutine) raises RuntimeError. Use `await main()` there instead.
Leftover tasks are cancelled when main returns, so fire-and-forget work gets killed silently at shutdown.
Python 3.11+ has `asyncio.Runner()` as a context manager. It reuses one loop across several `runner.run(coro)` calls.
Mistake: calling asyncio.run inside a loop or per request creates and tears down a loop every time. It is slow, and it breaks resources bound to a loop.
Mistake: asyncio objects made on one loop (Lock, Queue, client sessions) cannot be used from a different loop.

chapters.title: Awaitables: Coroutines, Tasks, Futures
points: An awaitable is any object usable in `await`: a coroutine, a Task, a Future, or any object with an `__await__` method that returns an iterator.
A coroutine runs only when awaited, sequentially, inside its caller. Awaiting it does not by itself create any concurrency.
A Future is a low-level placeholder for a result that will arrive later. It has states pending, done, and cancelled, and methods set_result, set_exception, and add_done_callback.
A Task is a Future subclass that wraps a coroutine and schedules it on the loop right away. It is the unit of concurrency.
`asyncio.create_task(coro, name=...)` starts the coroutine running concurrently. `await task` later retrieves its result.
Comparison row: a coroutine is lazy and sequential. A Task is eager, concurrent, and cancellable. A Future is a raw result slot and is usually created by library code.
`task.cancel()` injects CancelledError at the task's current await. `task.done()`, `task.result()`, and `task.exception()` let you inspect the outcome.
Futures are cheap to await more than once and support many awaiters. A bare coroutine can be awaited only once (a second await raises RuntimeError).
Mistake: the loop keeps only weak references to tasks. Store them (in a set, or in a TaskGroup), or they can be garbage-collected mid-run.
Mistake: an exception in a task that is never awaited is only logged as 'Task exception was never retrieved' when the task is garbage-collected.

chapters.title: How await Yields Control
points: An await chain goes down through nested coroutines until it reaches a Future that is still pending.
`Future.__await__` yields the Future object itself. That yield travels up through every `await` to the Task driving the chain.
The Task receives the Future, registers `add_done_callback(self.__wakeup)`, and returns to the loop. The whole coroutine stack is now suspended.
When I/O or a timer calls `fut.set_result(x)`, the callback schedules `Task.__step`, and `send()` resumes the coroutine right after the await.
Awaiting a coroutine that never reaches a pending Future does not yield at all. It runs straight through, like a normal function call.
`await asyncio.sleep(0)` is the explicit 'yield now' idiom. It does a bare yield so other ready tasks get a turn.
Example: two tasks each running `for i in range(3): print(name, i); await asyncio.sleep(0)` produce interleaved output: A0 B0 A1 B1 A2 B2.
Without that await, task A prints A0 A1 A2 and only then does B run. Switching happens only at points that actually suspend.
Mistake: a tight loop with no awaits (or with awaits that never suspend) starves the loop. Timeouts, heartbeats, and other clients all freeze.
Cancellation arrives only at a suspension point. A coroutine that never yields cannot be cancelled.

chapters.title: Running Things Concurrently
points: Sequential: `await a(); await b()` takes time(a) + time(b), even though both are async.
Concurrent: `await asyncio.gather(a(), b())` takes about max(time(a), time(b)) and returns results in argument order.
`gather(..., return_exceptions=True)` returns exceptions as values in the list instead of raising the first one.
Python 3.11+: `async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg: tg.create_task(a())`. The block waits for all tasks, and one failure cancels the siblings and raises an ExceptionGroup.

Comparison row: gather is simple and keeps result order, but by default a failure leaves the other tasks running. TaskGroup gives structured concurrency with safe cleanup, and is preferred in new code.
`asyncio.wait(tasks, return_when=FIRST_COMPLETED)` returns (done, pending) sets for fine-grained control. `asyncio.as_completed()` yields tasks in the order they finish.
Timeouts: `async with asyncio.timeout(5):` (3.11+) or `await asyncio.wait_for(coro, 5)`. Both raise TimeoutError and cancel the inner work.
Limit fan-out with `sem = asyncio.Semaphore(10)` and `async with sem:` so you don't open 10,000 sockets at once.
Mistake: `for u in urls: await fetch(u)` is fully sequential. Build the coroutines first, then pass them to gather or a TaskGroup.
Mistake: swallowing CancelledError in `except Exception` (fine since 3.8, when it became a BaseException) or with a bare `except:` breaks cancellation and timeouts.

chapters.title: Blocking Calls: to_thread and run_in_executor
points: A blocking call such as `time.sleep`, `requests.get`, sync DB drivers, or large file reads holds the only thread, so the whole loop and every task stall.
Rule: inside async code, use async libraries (aiohttp/httpx, asyncpg, aiofiles) or move the blocking call off the loop thread.
`await asyncio.to_thread(fn, *args, **kwargs)` (3.9+) runs fn in the default thread pool and awaits the result. It also copies contextvars.
`loop = asyncio.get_running_loop(); await loop.run_in_executor(None, fn, arg)`: None selects the default ThreadPoolExecutor.
run_in_executor takes only positional args. For keywords, use `functools.partial(fn, key=val)`.
You can pass a custom executor: `run_in_executor(ProcessPoolExecutor(), fn, x)` runs CPU work in real parallel processes, with picklable args and result.
Under the hood the executor returns a concurrent.futures.Future, which is wrapped with `asyncio.wrap_future` so the loop can await it.
Default pool size is min(32, os.cpu_count() + 4) workers. Too many simultaneous blocking calls queue up behind that limit.
Comparison row: to_thread is concise and threads only. run_in_executor is more verbose, but lets you pick a thread or process executor.
Mistake: cancelling a to_thread await does not stop the thread. The function keeps running to completion in the background.

chapters.title: Why CPU-Bound Work Doesn't Speed Up
points: asyncio runs all coroutines on one thread, so at any moment only one piece of Python code is executing.
CPU-bound code (hashing, parsing, number crunching) never waits, so it never yields. Wrapping it in `async def` adds overhead and gives no speedup.
Example: gather-ing 4 async functions that each spend 1 s on CPU still takes about 4 s total, and the loop is frozen the whole time.
Threads don't help pure-Python CPU work on standard CPython. The GIL lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time.
Exceptions: C extensions that release the GIL (NumPy, hashlib on large inputs, zlib) can run in parallel through to_thread.
The free-threaded CPython build (3.13t+, no GIL) allows real thread parallelism, but it is opt-in and not yet the default.
The fix is `ProcessPoolExecutor` through run_in_executor: one interpreter per core, so it scales with the core count.
Trade-off: processes pay startup cost plus pickling of arguments and results, so they only pay off for chunky tasks (tens of ms or more).
Middle ground: split a long CPU loop into chunks with `await asyncio.sleep(0)` between them. This keeps the loop responsive but does not make it faster.
Summary: I/O-bound → asyncio. Blocking library → to_thread. CPU-bound → processes. Mixed → an asyncio front end with a process pool behind it.

chapters.title: asyncio Cheatsheet
points: Define and run: `async def main(): ...` then `asyncio.run(main())`, called once, at the top level.
Sequential vs concurrent: `await a(); await b()` runs one after the other. `await asyncio.gather(a(), b())` runs them together.
Start background work: `t = asyncio.create_task(coro())`, keep a reference to it, and `await t` later.
Structured concurrency (3.11+): `async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg: tg.create_task(...)`.
Timeouts: `async with asyncio.timeout(s):` or `await asyncio.wait_for(coro, s)`, which raise TimeoutError.
Yield to the loop: `await asyncio.sleep(0)`. Never use `time.sleep()` in async code.
Blocking sync call: `await asyncio.to_thread(fn, *args)`. For CPU-heavy work: `await loop.run_in_executor(ProcessPoolExecutor(), fn, x)`.
Get the loop inside a coroutine with `asyncio.get_running_loop()`. From another thread, use `asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe(coro, loop)`.
Limit concurrency with `asyncio.Semaphore(n)`. Protect state shared across awaits with `asyncio.Lock()`. For producer/consumer, use `asyncio.Queue()`.
Red flags: 'coroutine was never awaited', a blocking call inside async def, swallowed CancelledError, unreferenced tasks, and asyncio.run inside a running loop.
